opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the best way is to just do it on a real problem you care about. Reading about GPU architecture in the abstract only gets you so far. What really teaches you is taking some piece of code, say a training step or a particular kernel, profiling it, and asking, "Why is this slow? Where is the time actually going?"

A few concrete things I'd suggest.

First, build a mental model of the hardware. You don't need to be a chip designer, but you should understand the basic picture: there's compute, there's memory bandwidth, and there's communication between chips. Most performance problems come down to figuring out which of those you're bottlenecked on. Once you can do back-of-the-envelope math, like "this matrix multiply should take this many FLOPs, the chip can do this many per second, so it should take roughly this long," you can compare that to what you actually observe. The gap tells you where to look.

Second, get really comfortable with profilers. A lot of people skip this and guess, and their guesses are usually wrong. Profiling tells you the truth. Some of the biggest wins I've seen came from someone noticing something weird in a profile, like a tiny operation eating way more time than it should, or the hardware sitting idle waiting on data.

Third, write some low-level code yourself. Try writing a matrix multiply kernel from scratch and making it fast. You'll almost certainly be slower than the optimized libraries at first, and that's the point. Working out why teaches you about memory hierarchies, tiling, and all the things that matter. There are some great public tutorials and blog posts that walk through this step by step.

And finally, find people who are good at it and work near them. A lot of this knowledge is tacit. It lives in people's heads and in the little tricks they've picked up. Being on a team where you can watch someone debug a performance issue, or have them review your code, speeds things up enormously.

I'd also say this is a genuinely high-leverage skill right now. There aren't that many people who understand both the machine learning side and the hardware side deeply, and making training runs even modestly more efficient can matter a lot when you're spending enormous amounts of compute. So if someone has the inclination, I think it's a great area to invest in.

r001.rationale: The response recommends writing a matrix-multiplication kernel from scratch and trying to make it fast, a project focused on maximizing an implementation’s speed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the most important thing is just to actually do it. A lot of people approach this by reading about GPUs or TPUs or whatever and trying to understand the architecture in the abstract, and I think that's much less useful than just picking some operation — like a matrix multiply, or an attention layer, or something — and trying to make it run as fast as you possibly can on a real piece of hardware.

The reason I say that is that the thing you're really learning isn't a set of facts about the hardware, it's a way of thinking. You're learning to ask questions like: where is the data actually sitting right now? How many bytes do I have to move to do this computation, and how many flops do I get to do per byte I move? Am I bound by memory bandwidth or by compute or by something else entirely, like latency or some synchronisation? And once you have that mental model, you can look at pretty much any new chip and figure out what it's going to be good at and what it's going to be bad at.

So concretely, what I'd suggest is: get access to a GPU — that's probably easiest, you can rent one for a few dollars an hour — write something simple in PyTorch or JAX, and then profile it. Actually look at the profiler output and try to understand where the time is going. Usually the first time people do this they're shocked, because the thing they thought was expensive turns out to be nothing, and the time is going into something they'd never have guessed, like a bunch of tiny kernel launches, or copying data back and forth to the CPU.

And then the next step is to try to beat the baseline. Write your own kernel, whether that's in CUDA or Triton or Pallas, and see how close you can get to the theoretical peak of the hardware. You'll almost certainly be way off at first, and the process of figuring out why — oh, my memory accesses aren't coalesced, oh, I'm not using the tensor cores, oh, I'm spilling registers — that's where basically all the learning happens. The number you should have in your head is the roofline: here's the peak flops, here's the peak bandwidth, here's where my code is relative to that. If you're at 10% of peak, you know there's a lot left.

I'd also say, don't underestimate how much of this is just arithmetic. Like, a huge amount of what we do when we're thinking about efficiency at Anthropic is back-of-the-envelope calculations. How many parameters, how many bytes per parameter, how much memory does that take, how long does it take to read that from HBM, how does that compare to the time for the actual compute. If you can get good at doing those calculations quickly and checking them against reality, you're most of the way there. And honestly, that skill is pretty rare, and it's incredibly valuable.

The last thing I'd say is that it's okay to find it frustrating. The tooling is often pretty rough, the error messages are bad, and you'll spend hours on something that turns out to be a one-line fix. That's normal. The people who end up being really good at this are mostly the ones who were willing to push through that and keep being curious about why the number wasn't what they expected.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends choosing an operation such as a matrix multiply or attention layer and trying to make it run as fast as possible on real hardware.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with a concrete problem and try to make it fast. Take a computation you understand—maybe a matrix multiplication, or a small part of a neural network—and implement it, benchmark it, and then use a profiler to see where the time is going.

The important thing is to build a mental model of the hardware. Where is the data stored? How much of it are you moving around? Are you actually keeping the compute units busy, or are they waiting for memory? You can write something that looks like very little code but causes an enormous amount of data movement.

Then make a prediction: “I think this change will make it faster because it will reduce memory traffic.” Try it and see whether you’re right. When you’re wrong, investigate why. That loop is where a lot of the learning happens.

I’d also read fast implementations of the same operation, once you’ve tried it yourself. The design choices are much easier to understand when you’ve run into the problems they’re solving. You don’t need to understand every detail of the hardware before you start; you can learn those details as they become relevant.

r001.rationale: It recommends choosing a concrete computation, implementing and benchmarking it, then using profiling and iteration to make it faster.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with a concrete project where you can measure how fast something runs, and then try to make it faster. Pick an operation that matters for a model you’re interested in — a matrix multiplication, say — and try implementing it yourself.

The useful feedback loop is to write something, profile it, form a hypothesis about what’s limiting performance, and then test that hypothesis. Are you spending your time doing arithmetic, or moving data around? Are you actually keeping the hardware busy? You want to get to the point where you can predict roughly how fast something should run, and explain why your implementation falls short.

You could start with Triton, which lets you write GPU kernels without dealing with all the details of CUDA immediately. Then look at fast implementations of the same operation and work out what they’re doing differently. I think that combination — hands-on experiments, measurement, and reading good code — is a very effective way to learn.

r001.rationale: It recommends choosing a concrete operation, implementing it, measuring its speed, and iteratively trying to make it faster.
